The evidence from d1, d2, d4, d5, and d6 uniformly describes that male brains have stronger front-to-back/intrahemispheric connections while female brains have stronger cross-hemispheric connections, linking these patterns to differences in cognitive tasks like single-task performance versus multitasking [d1, d2, d4, d5, d6]. d3 provides complementary evidence of a functional difference in response to infant cries, which aligns with the broader theme of sex-based brain differences without contradicting the wiring claims.

Based on the consistent evidence, the answer is that brains are wired differently. Yes, the brains of men and women are wired differently according to multiple studies [d1, d2, d5, d6]. Research using brain scans shows that male brains typically have stronger connections within each hemisphere (front-to-back), while female brains have stronger connections between the left and right hemispheres [d1, d2, d5, d6]. These structural differences are linked to observed cognitive tendencies, such as men often excelling at single tasks like navigation and women at multitasking and social cognition [d1, d4, d5]. Some experts caution that these generalizations are complex and brain connections can change [d1], but the core finding of wiring differences is consistently reported.
